**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 55, verses 1–4:**

﴿The Most Merciful * Taught the Qur'an﴾ This is an enumeration of a blessing upon the one whom God taught the Qur'an. It was also said: the meaning of "taught the Qur'an" is that He made it a sign and a proof for our master Muhammad (ﷺ). The first is more apparent. ﴿The Most Merciful﴾ is in the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and the verbs that follow it are successive predicates (akhbar mutawaliyah). This is indicated by their coming without a conjunction (harf 'atf). ﴿Created man﴾. It was said: he means the genus of mankind. It was said: he means Adam. It was said: he means our master Muhammad (ﷺ), and there is no evidence for restricting it. The first is more preferred. ﴿Taught him al-bayan﴾, meaning speech and articulation.

﴿The sun and the moon [move] by precise calculation﴾. That is, they both run in their orbit according to a known reckoning and a determined arrangement, and in this is a proof of the Wise Creator, the Willing, the All-Powerful.

﴿And the star and the tree prostrate themselves.﴾ According to Ibn ʿAbbas, al-najm (the star) is the plant that has no stem, such as herbs, and al-shajar (the tree) is the plant that has a stem. It is also said that al-najm is the category of the stars of the sky. Prostration (sujud) is an expression for humility and submission to God, the Exalted. It is also said that the prostration of the sun is its setting, and the prostration of the tree is its shadow.

﴿For the creatures﴾: i.e., for mankind. It is also said: for humankind and the jinn. And it is said: for all living creatures. "Al-akmam" (the sheaths): it may be the singular "kumm" with a damma on the kaf, which is the fibrous covering that wraps around the palm tree, and from it the sleeve of a shirt (qamis) is likened (to it); or it may be the plural of "kimm" with a kasra on the kaf, which is the casing of the fruit.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verse 13:

﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you two deny?﴾ Al-ala' (الآلاء) means: the blessings (al-ni'am). Its singular is "ilw" (إِلْى), on the pattern of "mi'y" (مِعْي). It is also said: "ala" (ألى), on the pattern of "qadaa" (قضى). And it is said: "alay" (أَلَيْ), on the pattern of "amad" (أمد) or on the pattern of "hasar" (حصر). The address is to both jinn and humankind (al-thaqalan), as evidenced by His saying: ﴿We will soon attend to you, O you two groups (al-thaqalan)﴾ [al-Rahman: 31]. It is narrated that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse, his companions remained silent, so he said: "The response of the jinn is better than your silence. When I recited it to the jinn, they said: 'We do not deny any of the favours of our Lord.'" He repeated this verse for emphasis and intensification. It is also said: each occurrence refers back to the meaning of the verse preceding it, so it is not mere emphasis, since emphasis does not exceed three repetitions.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verses 14–15:

﴿He created man from clay like pottery﴾. The man (al-insan) is Adam. Salsal (clay) is dry earth; when it is fired, it becomes fakhkhar (pottery). ﴿And He created the jann from a smokeless flame of fire﴾. The jann are the jinn, meaning Iblis, the father of the jinn. Marij is the quivering, agitated flame of fire.

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 55, verse 17:

﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾. He means the rising-points of the sun and the moon, and the setting-points of the sun and the moon. It is also said: the two rising-points and two setting-points of summer and winter.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verses 19–20:

﴿He let loose the two seas, meeting each other﴾. It was mentioned in Al-Furqan, meaning that the water of this one meets the water of that one. This happens when rain falls into the sea, according to the view that the sweet sea is the rain. As for the view that the sweet sea is the rivers and springs, their meeting is by the pouring of the rivers into the sea. As for the view of those who say that the two seas are the Persian Sea and the Roman Sea, or the Red Sea (al-Qulzum) and the Yemeni Sea, it is weak, because of His saying in Al-Furqan [53]: ﴿This one is sweet and palatable, and this one is salty and bitter﴾. Each of these is bitter. The meaning of "the two seas" in this surah is the same as what is meant in Al-Furqan. ﴿Between them is a barrier﴾, meaning a separating barrier, namely the body of the earth, or a barrier from the power of Allah. ﴿They do not transgress﴾, meaning neither of them transgresses upon the other by mixing. It was also said: they do not transgress upon the people by overflowing.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verse 22:

﴿From them both come out the pearl and the coral.﴾ Al-Lu'lu' (pearl) is the large of the gems, and al-Marjan (coral) is its small. It was also said: the reverse. And it was said: al-Marjan is red stones. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: "This is the correct view." As for His saying "from them both" while it comes out of only one of them, we have discussed it in Surah Fatir.

**﴿And His are the ships, raised high upon the sea, like mountains﴾**. He means the ships, and called them *munshaʼat* (raised up) because people bring them into being (*yunshi'ūnahā*). Ḥamzah and Abū Bakr read *al-munshiʼāt* with a kasra on the shīn, meaning that they produce the course (of the sea) or produce the waves. *Al-aʻlām* means the mountains; he likened the ships to them.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verses 26–27:

﴿Everyone upon it will perish﴾. The pronoun in "upon it" (ʿalayhā) refers to the earth; the context of the discourse indicates this, even though it has not been previously mentioned. By "whoever is upon it" he means the children of Adam and the other animals, but he gave precedence to the rational beings (al-ʿuqalāʾ).

﴿And there will remain the Face of your Lord, Owner of Majesty and Honour﴾. "The Face" (al-wajh) here is an expression for the Essence (al-dhāt). "Owner of Majesty" (dhū al-jalāl) is a description of the Essence, because among His names is al-Jalīl (the Majestic), and its meaning approaches that of al-ʿAẓīm (the Mighty). As for describing Him as "Honour" (al-ikrām), it may mean that He honours His servants, as He said in Surat al-Isrāʾ [70]: ﴿And We have certainly honoured the children of Adam﴾; or it may mean that His servants honour Him by affirming His Oneness, glorifying Him, and worshipping Him.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verse 29:

﴿Everyone in the heavens and the earth asks Him﴾ The meaning is that everyone in the heavens and the earth asks Allah for what they need. Some of them ask Him with the tongue of speech, and these are the believers; and some ask Him with the tongue of state (lisan al-hal), because all of them are in need of Him. ﴿Every day He is engaged in some affair﴾ The meaning is that He, exalted is He, exercises His dominion over His kingdom (malakut) in a manner that becomes manifest every day through giving and withholding, causing death and giving life, and other things. It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited it, and it was said to him, "What is that affair?" He said, "Among His affairs is that He forgives a sin, relieves a distress, raises up some people and lowers others." It was also asked of some of them: how can He say, ﴿Every day He is engaged in some affair﴾ when the pen has dried over what is to occur until the Day of Resurrection? He answered: He is engaged in an affair that He manifests, not in an affair that He initiates.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verse 31:

﴿Soon We shall attend to you, O you two worlds (ath-thaqalan)﴾. Its meaning is a warning, like your saying to one whom you threaten: "I will soon attend to your punishment." It does not mean freedom from some occupation. It may also mean that the duration of this world comes to an end, and at that time its affair concludes, so that nothing remains but the affair of the Hereafter; this is expressed by "attending" (al-tafarrugh).

Imam Ja'far ibn Muhammad said: The jinn and mankind were called "two burdens" (thaqalan) as if they were weighed down by sins.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verse 33:

﴿If you are able to pass through the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass through; you will not pass through except with authority.﴾

This is a statement addressed to the jinn and mankind on the Day of Resurrection, meaning: if you are able to flee and escape beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then do so. It is related that on that day they will try to flee because of what they see of the terrors of the Resurrection, but they will find seven rows of angels that have surrounded the earth, so they will turn back. It was also said: rather, they were addressed with this in the world; and the meaning is: if you are able to escape from the subjugation of Allah and His decree over you, then do so. His saying ﴿then pass through﴾ is a command intended to show their incapacity (al-ta'jiz). ﴿You will not pass through except with authority﴾ means: you are not able to pass through except by strength, and you have no strength.

﴿A flame of fire and brass will be sent upon you both﴾. Al-shuwāẓ is the blazing flame of fire, and al-nuḥās is smoke. It is also said that it is copper (al-ṣufr), melted and poured over their heads. Shuwāẓ is recited with a ḍamma on the shīn, and Ibn Kathīr recited it with a kasra. Both are two dialects (lughatān). Nuḥās is also recited with a rafʿ (nominative), as a continuation of shuwāẓ, and with a khafḍ (genitive), as an ʿaṭf (conjunction) on nār.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verse 37:

﴿When the sky splits asunder﴾ The answer (jawab) of ﴿idha﴾ (when) is his saying: ﴿then on that day﴾. And Ibn ʿAtiyya said: its answer is omitted. ﴿And it will become red like a rose, like oil⁠—﴾ The meaning of "warda" is red, like the rose. It was also said that it is from the color of a horse called "ward" (rose-colored). Qatada said: the sky is green today, and on the Day of Resurrection it will be red. "Al-dihan" is the plural of "dahn" (oil), like olive oil and the like. The sky on the Day of Resurrection was likened to it because it melts from the intensity of the terror. It was also said: its shining is likened to the shining of oil. And it was also said: "al-dihan" is red leather.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verse 39:

﴿So on that Day, neither man nor jinn will be asked about his sin.﴾ The questioning that is negated here is questioning in the sense of inquiry and seeking information, or seeking forgiveness, since that is not needed. This is because the criminals are recognized by their marks (sima), and because their deeds are known to Allah and recorded in their scrolls (suhuf). As for the questioning that is affirmed in His words: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ [al-Hijr: 92] and elsewhere, it is questioning in the sense of reckoning (hisab) and rebuke (tawbikh). So there is no contradiction between the negated and the affirmed. It has been said: this is due to the difference of the situations (mawatin), and the first view is better.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verses 41–43:

﴿The criminals will be known by their marks﴾. That is, by their sign, which is blackness of the faces and other things. "The criminals" here means the disbelievers, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿This is Hell, which the criminals used to deny﴾. ﴿They will be seized by the forelocks and the feet﴾. It was said: its meaning is that some of the disbelievers will be seized by their forelocks and others by their feet. And it was said: rather, each one will be seized by his forelock and his feet, then he will be folded up and thrown into the Fire.

**Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on Surah 55 (ar-Rahman), verses 46–48:**

﴿And for him who fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens.﴾ "The standing before his Lord" means standing before Him for the reckoning, as in His words: ﴿The day when mankind will stand before the Lord of the worlds﴾ (Al-Mutaffifin 83:6). It was also said that it means [that Allah will call him to account] for his deeds, as in His words: ﴿Is then He who stands over every soul in what it has earned [like those who associate partners with Him]?﴾ (Ar-Ra'd 13:33). It was also said that the meaning is "for him who fears his Lord," and the word "standing" (maqam) has been inserted, as when you say: "I feared the side of so-and-so" (kharaftu janib fulan).

Scholars differed over whether the two gardens are for each individual fearer separately, or for the group of fearers as a class. This depends on whether the phrase ﴿for him who fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens﴾ intends one person or a group.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "He said 'two gardens' because He addressed both the two weighty groups (ath-thaqalayn, humankind and jinn), so it is as if He said: a garden for mankind and a garden for the jinn."

﴿Both having many branches﴾: here the word "dhawat" (possessors of) is in the dual form, returning to its original form, because its root is "dhawat," as Ibn 'Atiyya said. "Al-afnan" is the plural of "fann," which is a branch (ghusn), or the plural of "fann," which is a kind (sinf) of fruits and other things.

﴿Of every fruit there are two kinds﴾, meaning two types. ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near at hand﴾. Al-janā is what is picked of fruits, and dānin means near. It is reported that a person can pick the fruit in Paradise in any position, whether standing, sitting, or reclining, because it hangs down for him whenever he wants it. In His words ﴿wa-janā al-jannatayn﴾ there is a form of tajnīs (paronomasia, the figure in which two words share a similar form but differ in meaning).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verses 56–58:

﴿Restraining their glances﴾. This was mentioned in al-Saffat [37:48]. ﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them.﴾ The meaning is that they are virgins. "Lam yatmithhunna" (lam yaṭmithhunna) means he did not deflower them. It has been said that al-ṭamth (ṭamth) means intercourse, whether with a virgin or someone other than a virgin. The negation that a human or a jinn has touched them is for emphasis and to indicate generality, as if He said that nothing has touched them. It has also been said that He meant: human women were not touched by humans, and jinn women were not touched by jinn. This view implies that jinn enter Paradise and enjoy in it what humans enjoy. ﴿As if they were rubies and coral.﴾ The women are likened to rubies and coral in redness and beauty. We have already mentioned coral at the beginning of the surah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verses 56–58:

﴿Restraining their glances﴾. This was mentioned in al-Saffat [37:48]. ﴿No man or jinn has touched them before them.﴾ The meaning is that they are virgins. "Lam yatmithhunna" (lam yaṭmithhunna) means he did not deflower them. It has been said that al-ṭamth (ṭamth) means intercourse, whether with a virgin or someone other than a virgin. The negation that a human or a jinn has touched them is for emphasis and to indicate generality, as if He said that nothing has touched them. It has also been said that He meant: human women were not touched by humans, and jinn women were not touched by jinn. This view implies that jinn enter Paradise and enjoy in it what humans enjoy. ﴿As if they were rubies and coral.﴾ The women are likened to rubies and coral in redness and beauty. We have already mentioned coral at the beginning of the surah.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verse 60:

﴿Is the recompense of good anything but good?﴾ The meaning is that the recompense of the one who does good through obedience to God is that God does good to him by (granting him) the Garden. It is also possible that "good" (al-ihsan) here is the same as what Gabriel asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about, and he said to him: "That you worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, then He sees you," and that is the station of watchfulness (muraqabah) and witnessing (mushahadah). So the recompense for that good is these two gardens. What strengthens this is that He made these two gardens described here for the people of the lofty station, and made two gardens below them for those who are below that level. So the two gardens mentioned first are for the foremost (al-sabiqun), and the two gardens mentioned second, after that, are for the companions of the right (ashab al-yamin), as stated in Surah al-Waqi'ah. Consider how He made the attributes of these two gardens higher than the attributes of the two gardens after them. He said here: "two springs flowing," and said of the other two: "two gushing springs" (naddakhatan), and flowing (al-jary) is stronger than gushing (al-nadkh). He said there: "of every fruit, two kinds," and said here: "fruit, and date palms, and pomegranates." Likewise, the description of the maidens (hur) here is more eloquent than their description there. Likewise the description of the spreading out (al-bast) is that, the saying of the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Two gardens of gold, their vessels and everything in them, and two gardens of silver, their vessels and everything in them."
﴿Mudhammatān﴾ means: deeply dark green, tending toward blackness because of the intensity of their greenness.

﴿In them are two gushing springs﴾. Meaning: they gush forth with water. The word النضخ (*al-nadkh*), with the dotted خاء (*kha'*), is stronger in meaning than النضح (*al-nadh*), with the undotted حاء (*ha'*).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verse 68:

﴿Fruit, and palm trees, and pomegranates﴾. He singled out the palm and the pomegranate for mention after their inclusion within "fruit," to honour them and to show their excellence over the rest of the fruits. This is what is called al-tajrid (the rhetorical device of isolating a part after its inclusion in the whole).

﴿Khayrātun ḥisān: good and beautiful [women]﴾. *Khayrāt* is the plural of *khayra*. Al-Zamakhsharī and others said: its original form is *khayyirāt* with doubling (*tashdīd*), and then it was lightened, as in كَمْيت (*kumayt*). It was also read with doubling.

Umm Salama said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me about His words, the Exalted: ﴿good and beautiful [women]﴾." He (ﷺ) said: "Good characters and beautiful faces."

Ibn Juzayy's commentary (al-Tashil) on Surah 55, verse 72:

﴿Maidens, cloistered in pavilions﴾. "Hur" (ḥūr) is the plural of "ḥawrā'" (ḥawrā'), and "maqṣūrāt" means those who are kept hidden (secluded). This is because women are praised for remaining in their homes and blamed for frequent going out. "Khiyām" (khiyām, pavilions) are the dwellings made of wood, grass and the like, while the pavilions of Paradise are made of pearls.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 55, verse 76:

﴿Reclining on green cushions﴾. *Al-rafraf* (الرفرف) means the spreads (carpets or rugs). It is also said to mean the cushions, and it is also said to mean the gardens of Paradise. ﴿And beautiful couches﴾. *Al-'abqari* (العبقري) means the fine carpets (*tanafis*). It is also said to mean the *zarabi* (fine rugs), and it is also said to mean thick brocade (*dibaj*). It is attributed to *'Abqar*, and the Arabs claim that it is the land of the jinn. So when they admire something, they attribute it to it.

﴿Blessed is the name of your Lord﴾ The verb *tabaraka* (blessed, exalted) has been mentioned in *al-Furqan* (the Criterion, Surah 25) and elsewhere. Here, according to the most apparent view, "the name" (*al-ism*) is intended to mean the one who is named (*al-musamma*). The majority of reciters (*al-Jumhur*) read ذي الجلال with a *yāʾ*, as an adjective (*sifa*) of *Rabbika* (your Lord). Ibn ʿĀmir read it with a *wāw*, as an adjective of *al-ism* (the name). The meaning of ذي الجلال والإكرام (Owner of Majesty and Honour) has already been mentioned.
